item.title: Go Daily Question 20250603
item.description:
What is the output of the following code? Why?

func main() {

 var m = [...]int{1, 2, 3}

 for i, v := range m {
 go func() {
 fmt.Println(i, v)
 }()
 }

 time.Sleep(time.Second * 3)
}
🔑 Answer Analysis:

Before Go 1.22: 2 3 2 3 2 3 The for range loop uses short variable declaration (:=) to iterate variables. It’s important to note that variables i and v are reused in each loop iteration, not re-declared.

item.title: Go Daily Question 166
item.description:
Yesterday there were only 3 G’s. What would be the output if the number of G’s was changed to 257?

package main

import (
 "fmt"
 "runtime"
 "sync"
)

func main() {
 runtime.GOMAXPROCS(1)

 var wg sync.WaitGroup
 wg.Add(257)
 for i := 1; i <= 257; i++ {
 go func(i int) {
 fmt.Println(i)
 wg.Done()
 }(i)
 }
 wg.Wait()
}
🔑 Answer Analysis:

Run online

257
1
2
3
...
255
256

The result is consistent with the case of 3 Goroutines, because the local runq’s capacity limit is 256. When G257 is added to P, it will enter the runnext slot (the clip has a maximum capacity of 256, but one bullet can be chambered. Thus, up to 257).

item.title: Go Daily Question 165
item.description:
What is the output of the following code and explain it?

package main

import (
 "runtime"
 "sync"
)

func main() {
 runtime.GOMAXPROCS(1)

 var wg sync.WaitGroup
 wg.Add(3)
 go func(n int) {
 println(n)
 wg.Done()
 }(1)
 go func(n int) {
 println(n)
 wg.Done()
 }(2)
 go func(n int) {
 println(n)
 wg.Done()
 }(3)
 wg.Wait()
}
🔑 Answer Analysis:

Run online

3
1
2

Brief explanation: A go function creates a new Goroutine (G). Each Processor (P) has a record of the next G to run and a local queue (like loading a pistol). G1, G2, G3 enter P sequentially. Eventually, the next G to run is G3, and G1, G2 are in the queue.

 go fmt.Println(<-ch1)
 ch1 <- 5

  • B: Cannot compile
  • C: Runtime deadlock

C Run online

fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!

item.title: Go Daily Question 130
item.description:
What’s wrong with the following code?

package main

import (
 "sync"
)

const N = 10

var wg = &sync.WaitGroup{}

func main() {
 for i := 0; i < N; i++ {
 go func(i int) {
 wg.Add(1)
 println(i)
 defer wg.Done()
 }(i)
 }
 wg.Wait()
}
🔑 Answer Analysis:

Why is there no output after running? The purpose of a WaitGroup is to wait for a collection of goroutines to finish. It maintains an internal counter. The Add method increments the internal counter by delta. The Done method decrements the WaitGroup counter. The Wait method blocks until the WaitGroup counter becomes zero.

item.title: Go Daily Question 044
item.description:
What’s wrong with the following code, and how to fix it?

total, sum := 0, 0
for i := 1; i <= 10; i++ {
 sum += i
 go func() {
 total += i
 }()
}
fmt.Printf("total:%d sum %d", total, sum)
🔑 Answer Analysis:

The value of sum is 55. The value of total is between 55 and 100 (inclusive).

Point 1: Know what the output effect is and how to solve it. Point 2: Data race. Because multiple goroutines are writing to the total variable simultaneously, there is a data race. Point 3: The main function exits first, and the launched goroutines do not get a chance to execute.

item.title: Go Daily Question 038
item.description:
What is wrong with the following code?

package main

import (
 "sync"
)

const N = 10

var wg = &sync.WaitGroup{}

func main() {
 for i := 0; i < N; i++ {
 go func(i int) {
 wg.Add(1)
 println(i)
 defer wg.Done()
 }(i)
 }
 wg.Wait()
}
🔑 Answer Analysis:

Answer: The output is not unique, and the code has risks; not all go statements may be executed. Analysis:

var wg = &sync.WaitGroup{}
wg.Add(1)
wg.Done()
wg.Wait()

This usage is similar to a stack. wg.Wait() checks if there are any records in wg. If there are, it blocks until the stack becomes 0 before becoming active. The way it’s written here has a problem. wg.Add(1) is placed inside the goroutine, which means wg.Wait() might evaluate before wg.Add(1) has been executed for all goroutines.

item.title: Go Daily Question 037
item.description:
What happens when the following code is executed?

package main

import (
 "fmt"
 "time"
)

func main() {
 ch := make(chan int, 1000)
 go func() {
 for i := 0; i < 10; i++ {
 ch <- i
 }
 }()
 go func() {
 for {
 a, ok := <-ch
 if !ok {
 fmt.Println("close")
 return
 }
 fmt.Println("a: ", a)
 }
 }()
 close(ch)
 fmt.Println("ok")
 time.Sleep(time.Second * 100)
}
🔑 Answer Analysis:

Answer: Prints “ok” then panics. It takes time to start goroutines. Here, the close(ch) statement closes the channel. Writing data to an already closed channel will cause a program panic.
